items.bodyEn: Odawara was the stronghold of the Hōjō clan until Toyotomi Hideyoshi's siege of 1590. Under the Tokugawa it stayed a castle town and the largest post town in Sagami, the last big stop before the Hakone climb. Hiroshige's print shows travelers carried over the bridgeless Sakawa River on porters' shoulders, castle and mountains beyond.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō series (c. 1833), print 'Odawara: Sakawa River' (酒匂川)

items.bodyEn: The Odawara lantern is a slim paper cylinder on bamboo hoops that collapses flat into its own wooden lid, so a traveler could tuck it into a sleeve or pack by day and light it for the Hakone road at night. It became a craft of the town in the Edo period and remains its best-known souvenir.

items.titleEn: ください: Something Comes Down
items.bodyEn: ください, which you now use in 〜をください, is the request form of くださる, the respectful verb meaning to give. It is built on 下, down: a gift from someone above you comes down to your level. Asking with ください therefore politely places the other person higher, which is why it suits shops and strangers.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien (Iwanami), entry ください: 「くださる」の命令形「くだされ」の転

items.bodyEn: The kanji 北, north, began as a picture of two people standing back to back and meant simply the back, or to turn away. Because houses in ancient China faced south, the back was the north side, and the character took that meaning. A new character, 背, with a flesh element added, was later made for the body's back.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entry 北: 乖也, 从二人相背; Kanjigen (Gakken)
